name: Dawik Kui
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.note: Glottolog entry retired, kept for bookkeeping only; no references listed

new_statements.quote: [Winfield 1928: 10-11] 4. Accent. The accent or stress in a word generally falls upon the root, no matter what additions are made to it. E.g., kasa, to bite. (Root kas-.) kasite, it bit. kasinari, a thing that bites. Usually the stress is slight and the other syllables follow evenly without accentuation. But occasionally in speech the stress is increased remarkably by the vehemence of the speaker ... Occasionally the second syllable and not the root is accented in emphatic statements. E.g., dehane, many. dehane [accent on 2nd], very many. [Friend-Pereira 1909: 5] Accent in Kui, as in the other Dravidian languages, is on the syllable that constitutes the base of the word prior to the addition of formatives and inflexional forms
new_statements.citation: Winfield, W. W. 1928. A Grammar of the Kui Language. (Bibliotheca Indica, Work No. 245.) Calcutta: Asiatic Society of Bengal. Corroborating: Friend-Pereira, J. E. 1909. A Grammar of the Kui Language. Calcutta: Bengal Secretariat Book Depot, p. 5.
new_statements.locator: Winfield 1928, ch. II 'Roots', sec. 4 'Accent', pp. 10-11; dialect coverage statement Introduction pp. xiii-xiv. Friend-Pereira 1909, Part I 'Letters and Sounds', p. 5.
new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Files checked under (all present, lists file->citation->URL). (1) lines 1682-1721 (printed pp. 10-11, ch. II 'Roots', sec. '4. Accent'): the passage is there as quoted — 'The accent or stress in a word generally falls upon the root, no matter what additions are made to it. E.g., kasa, to bite. (Root kas-.) kasite, it bit. kasinari, a thing that bites. Usually the stress is slight and the other syllables follow evenly without accentuation. But occasionally in speech the stress is increased remarkably by the vehemence of the speaker.. Occasionally the second syllable and not the root is accented in enrphatic [sic scanned] statements. E.g., d£hane, many. dehane, very many. rdhona/roh6na, degit…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent sits on the root (base) syllable and stays there whatever suffixes are added; Kui is exclusively suffixing and roots are word-initial, so this amounts to initial stress. Stress is weak; the remaining syllables are even.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described ('the other syllables follow evenly without accentuation').
new_statements.exceptions: Emphatic/affective speech: the root syllable may be exaggerated and lengthened (sah-tatenju, roosi, oomba), or the accent may shift to the second syllable to intensify meaning (dehane 'many' vs 'very many', rohona 'always' vs 'for ever', degitenju 'he ran away' vs 'ran for his life').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement ('in a word'), illustrated on citation forms and inflected words; the shifts described are expressive/pragmatic, not phrasal rules. NB the description is of standard Kui (Gumsur-Udayagiri Taluk; Friend-Pereira: Khondmals), not of the Dawik/Gajapati (Chinna Kimedi) variety specifically; Winfield asserts grammatical uniformity across all Kui districts including Chinna Kimedi but makes no locality-specific remark about accent.
new_statements.identity_note: dawi1234 'Dawik Kui' [dwk] is a retired Glottolog bookkeeping code (category 'Pending Report Release') created after ISO 639-3 CR 2019-005 split Kui [kxu] into Kui (India) [uki] and Dawik Kui [dwk] on the strength of an unpublished NLCI survey; it denotes the Kui spoken in the Dawik region of Gajapati (the request form also says Ganjam) district, Odisha — the area the older grammars call the 'Chinna Kimedi dialect' of Kui. Glottolog and Wikipedia fold it into Kui (India) = kuii1252, which is ALREADY in our catalog from exactly the source quoted here (Winfield 1928 + Friend-Pereira 1909, root = initial stress). No description of the Dawik/Gajapati variety itself exists; every stress statement found is for standard Kui (Winfield: Gumsur-Udayagiri Taluk; Friend-Pereira: Khondmals), with Winfield asserting that grammatical construction is 'fundamentally the same' in all districts including Chinna Kimedi and the 1902/1906/1909 sources recording only segmental (d > l) and pronominal differences for Chinna Kimedi. by our rule that each source is filed under the language's current Glottolog code (a retired code does not make a separate language) this key should not become a separate catalog entity; at most it is an alias of kuii1252.

new_statements.quote: There is no phonemic stress in any of the Dravidian languages. Normally stress (loudness) falls on the initial syllable of a word, short or long. A non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels. Words can begin with vowels or consonants.
new_statements.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju. 2003. The Dravidian Languages. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press (ch. 2 phonology, Kui-Kuvi sections).
new_statements.locator: p. 27, sec. 1.5.1 'Phonology' (ch. 1 'Introduction'; p. 30 of the ch. 1 file; running heads '26 Introduction' / '28 Introduction' bracket the page). Ch. 2 sec. 2.4.1 'Stress and intonation' (p. 58) known only from a Google Books snippet (file).
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: 30 carries the running head '1.5 Typological features of Dravidian 27' and sec. 1.5.1 'Phonology' contains, word for word, 'There is no phonemic stress in any of the Dravidian languages. Normally stress (loudness) falls on the initial syllable of a word, short or long. A non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels. Words can begin with vowels or consonants.' (the only difference is the line-break hyphen in 'non-initial', which raw extracted text joins as 'noninitial'). p. 31 (= book p. 28, running head '28 Introduction') has 'Short vowels in non-root syllables (in unaccented position) tend to be lost', and sec. 1.5.2 opens 'There are no prefixes or infixes. Grammatical relations are…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Winfield 1928 statement (stress on the root, unchanged by suffixation): Dravidian words are suffix-only, so the root syllable is the initial syllable, and Krishnamurti's family-wide 'initial syllable' placement coincides with Winfield's root placement. It adds (a) that stress is not phonemic anywhere in Dravidian, (b) a weight note (non-initial long vowels are louder), (c) that unaccented non-root short vowels tend to be lost. Not Kui-specific: the p. 25 Kui entry (no. 14: Ganjam and Phulbani districts; Letchmajee 1853 first grammar; Winfield 1928/1929 still the main source) says nothing about stress. IMPORTANT for the catalog's open_url: the listed archive.org…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-wide statement, not Kui-specific: stress is not phonemic (non-contrastive) in any Dravidian language; the loudness peak normally sits on the first syllable of the word regardless of its length; a non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels (a phonetic weight effect, not a shift of the stress rule). p. 28 adds that short vowels in non-root syllables '(in unaccented position) tend to be lost', i.e. the root (= first) syllable is the accented one.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the text opened; only 'a non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels' (phonetic prominence of long vowels, not a secondary-stress rule).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Kui. Ch. 2 sec. 2.4.1 (p. 58, snippet only) says 'Very little has been written about stress and intonation' and cites the Tamil statement 'Stress in Tamil is non-contrastive, and falls on the first syllable of a word' (Annamalai and Steever 1998: 104) as typical. The Kui-Kuvi sections of ch. 2 were not obtainable (not held by the project, not open online).' block page stopped further queries.
new_statements.identity_note: ISO 639-3 dwk Dawik Kui = Kui of the Dawik region, Gajapati district (CR 2019-005 split of kxu into uki + dwk); Glottolog keeps dawi1234 as a Bookkeeping / Pending Report Release languoid with no description. Krishnamurti 2003 describes Kui as one language (entry 14, p. 25: Ganjam and Phulbani districts, standard sources Letchmajee 1853 and Winfield 1928/1929 = Gumsur-Udayagiri / Khondmals Kui) and his stress sentence is family-wide; no statement about the Dawik/Gajapati (older 'Chinna Kimedi') variety specifically exists in anything opened.

sources.note: Ch. II sec. 4 'Accent', pp. 10-11: 'The accent or stress in a word generally falls upon the root, no matter what additions are made to it' (kasa, kasite, kasinari, root kas-); stress slight, other syllables even; emphatic speech may exaggerate the first syllable or occasionally shift accent to the second syllable (dehane 'many' vs 'very many'). Standard = Kui of Gumsur-Udayagiri Taluk; Introduction (p. xiii-xiv) lists Chinna Kimedi (the Gajapati area) among Kui districts and says 'grammatical construction in all districts is fundamentally the same'.

sources.citation: Friend-Pereira, J. E. 1909. A Grammar of the Kui Language. Calcutta: Bengal Secretariat Book Depot. 89 pp. (archive.org grammarofkuilang00frierich, djvu text)
sources.note: Part I 'Letters and Sounds', p. 5: 'Accent in Kui, as in the other Dravidian languages, is on the syllable that constitutes the base of the word prior to the addition of formatives and inflexional forms, e.g., in gi-ppk-i-nenju, he is doing, the accent is on gippk.' Describes Kandh Mals (Khondmals) Kui with notes on Gumsar and Chinna Kimedi dialect forms.

sources.note: Nothing. Establishes identity only: Dawik Kui = Kui variety of the Dawik region of Gajapati (also 'Ganjam') district, 41-73% lexical similarity with Kandhamal Kui; sole basis an unpublished NLCI survey (Ngwazah, Behera & Majhi 2013); 'Not much information is available about this language, since it is counted as Kui language.'
